highlights: The Emperor's New Year Rescript reaffirmed the Meiji Charter Oath and explicitly renounced imperial divinity, while SCAP's 4 January directives ordered militarists removed from office and ultra-nationalist organizations abolished, forcing a Shidehara Cabinet reshuffle.

The International Military Tribunal for the Far East was established by proclamation and its Charter approved; SCAP ordered 171 war crimes suspects arrested, including Koki Hirota and Yosuke Matsuoka.
The first Yokohama war atrocity trials concluded with two death sentences and one life imprisonment sentence.
SCAP directed Japan to abrogate laws permitting licensed prostitution and annul contracts binding women to it.

Allied authorities impounded 394 industrial plants, including 294 aircraft and arsenal facilities, as the first step in interim reparations; 41 companies including Oji Paper were added to the Zaibatsu schedule.

Bank of Japan note issue reached a record ¥56 billion as direct government overdraft borrowing was halted; coal output rose 41 percent, though government rice collections stood at only 20 percent of quotas.
Labor unions expanded at two per day and planned a national federation, while a Tokyo survey found half of food came from black markets and Hokkaido cities held as little as two days of staples.

USAMGIK was formally established in Southern Korea, where nationwide protests and strikes opposed the Moscow Conference trusteeship agreement, and rice hoarding and coal shortages strained the economy.

sections.summary: The 4 January purge directives forced reorganization of the Shidehara Cabinet; the Emperor renounced divinity, licensed prostitution was abolished, elections were scheduled, and Yokohama war crimes trials concluded.
sections.title: Political Activities in Japan

sections.summary: Allied custody covered 394 industrial plants for reparations; coal output rose 41 percent; Bank of Japan note issue reached ¥56 billion; capital levy and war-profit tax bills were drafted.
sections.title: Economic Activities in Japan

sections.summary: A Tokyo survey found half of food came from black markets; typhus was checked while smallpox spread; 143 textbooks were cleared of militarism; professional educators were appointed to the Education Ministry.

sections.summary: USAMGIK took direct control of local military government units; anti-trusteeship demonstrations spread; a Korean constabulary was formed; emergency rice collection struggled against hoarding.

sections.summary: Japan's political affairs: the purge and Cabinet reshuffle, the Imperial Rescript, police and censorship measures, the Charter of the International Military Tribunal, 171 war crimes arrests and Yokohama death sentences.
sections.title: Part II: Political - Japan

sections.summary: The purge directives prompted a major Shidehara Cabinet and local government reshuffle; the Emperor's rescript denied divinity; Sanzo Nozaka returned from exile; Japan's administrative authority was limited to the four main islands.
sections.title: Government and Civil Administration

sections.summary: Authorities fought black markets and lethal bootleg whiskey, abolished the Keihei-tai auxiliary police while arming civil police with revolvers, interned ex-Ambassador Stahmer, and required censorship screening of all motion pictures.
sections.title: Public Safety and Intelligence

sections.summary: The Supreme Commander approved the Far East Tribunal's Charter; SCAP ordered 171 war crimes suspects arrested, including Koki Hirota and Yosuke Matsuoka; Yokohama commissions imposed two death sentences.
sections.title: Legal and War Crimes

sections.summary: Japan's economy: rice collection at 20 percent of quotas, coal up 41 percent, 394 plants held for reparations, unions growing, ¥56 billion note issue, and 41 firms added to the Zaibatsu schedule.
sections.title: Part III: Economic - Japan

sections.summary: Government rice collections reached only 20 percent of quotas amid black markets; the Agricultural Association Law was amended toward democratization; a fuel-oil link system was set up to stimulate fish deliveries.
sections.title: Agriculture and Fisheries

sections.summary: Charcoal and lumber shortages hampered heating and reconstruction; coal production rebounded 41 percent after increased miner rations; geological surveys assessed nonferrous metal, cement and quarrying capacity.
sections.title: Forestry and Mining

sections.summary: Allied authorities took custody of 394 aircraft plants, arsenals and laboratories for reparations; coal shortages suppressed iron, steel, chemical, textile and motor vehicle output despite new housing construction targets.
sections.title: Industry

sections.summary: Railroads suffered neglected rolling stock while electrification and fare increases were planned; shipping stood at a quarter of prewar capacity; electric power consumption rose sharply from residential heating.
sections.title: Transportation and Public Utilities

sections.summary: Foreign trade ran strictly under SCAP direction; U.S. Army surplus flour, diesel oil and medicines were imported; raw silk, coal, pitch and mining timbers went to Korea, China and Hong Kong.
sections.title: Imports and Exports

sections.summary: Unions grew at two per day and planned a national federation; substantial wage increases offset rising living costs; an official registration counted 32.7 million employed and 3.3 million unemployed.
sections.title: Labor

sections.summary: International radio and telephone circuits to the United States and Britain were restored; signal facilities supported occupation forces; a goal of 2.1 million radio receivers was set despite vacuum tube shortages.
sections.title: Communications

sections.summary: Staple food collections lagged, leaving Hokkaido cities with as little as two days of reserves; the government abandoned vegetable auctions and reimposed official ceiling prices on perishable foods.
sections.title: Rationing and Price Control

sections.summary: Bank of Japan note issue hit a record ¥56 billion; direct government overdraft borrowing was halted; commercial banks limited credit to essential producers; closed colonial and Axis financial institutions were liquidated.
sections.title: Money and Banking

sections.summary: SCAP ordered fiscal retrenchment and abolition of the Special Account for War Expenses; capital levy and war profit tax drafts were prepared; 41 companies including Oji Paper joined the Zaibatsu schedule.
sections.title: Public Finance

sections.summary: Japan's social affairs: relief and migration controls, smallpox vaccination, repatriation figures, appointment of educators to the Education Ministry, textbook screening, severing Shinto from the state, and media campaigns.
sections.title: Part IV: Social - Japan

sections.summary: SCAP curbed rural-to-urban migration; the Welfare Ministry estimated 8,000,000 people needed relief; smallpox prompted nationwide vaccination; repatriation processed over 1.2 million returnees and 720,000 departing foreign nationals.
sections.title: Public Health and Welfare

sections.summary: Professional educators were appointed to head the Ministry of Education; English translations were required for textbook screening; Shinto was severed from state control; media explained SCAP's political purge.
sections.title: Education, Religion and Media of Expression

sections.summary: Southern Korea under USAMGIK: Moscow Agreement protests and strikes, stalled coalition talks, Special Judicial Officers, constabulary recruitment, rice hoarding, trade licensing, coal shortages and refugee relief.
sections.title: Part V: Korea

sections.summary: Strikes and turmoil followed the Moscow Agreement's trusteeship announcement; Right-Left coalition talks stalled; USAMGIK created Special Judicial Officers; recruitment began for the Korean Constabulary.
sections.title: Political Activities in Korea

sections.summary: Rice hoarding persisted despite ceiling prices and incentives; foreign trade came under rigid licensing; the Chosen Stock Exchange was dissolved; coal shortages from Japan crippled southern Korean manufacturing.
sections.title: Economic Activities in Korea

sections.summary: Committees drafted democratic school programs; free civic newspapers passed one million circulation; procedures were set to recover cultural property taken by Japan; relief and disease control aided northern refugees.
sections.title: Social Activities in Korea

summary: Summation No. 4 documents non-military activities in Japan and American-occupied Korea during January 1946, marking a pivotal phase of early postwar transformation. In Japan, the Occupation accelerated institutional democratization through the landmark 4 January purge directives, the Emperor’s New Year rescript renouncing divinity, the abolition of licensed prostitution, and preparations for national elections. Allied authorities promulgated the Charter for the International Military Tribunal for the Far East, completed initial war crimes trials in Yokohama, and impounded 394 industrial plants for reparations. Concurrently, Japan confronted severe socioeconomic distress: acute food shortages, rampant black markets, and an expanding Bank of Japan note issue, counterbalanced by surging labor unionization and recovering coal production. In Southern Korea, the formal establishment of USAMGIK was overshadowed by massive public unrest following the Moscow Conference trusteeship announcement, while severe coal shortages and rice hoarding paralyzed the economy. For historians, this summation provides extraordinary empirical baselines: complete tabulations of Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Yasuda, and Sumitomo corporate subsidiaries, 20-year trends in agricultural output, national employment census data, nationwide disease maps, and the structural reorganization of Japanese education and police administration.
